It is: οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν "nothing at all existed." And the restriction is supplied by the referent of the πραγματεία, not by an adjective I am entitled to insert into Aristotle's claim. So the structure is: Ταύτης ... τῆς πραγματείας of this inquiry οὐ ... προεξειργασμένον not worked out beforehand ἀλλ᾽ οὐδὲν παντελῶς ὑπῆρχεν but nothing at all existed. The total is restricted by "of this inquiry". It is not subsequently weakened by "systematic," "fully developed," "formal," "comparable," or any of the other scholarly cushions I introduced. And then I compounded the problem by saying: "What they didn't have ... was the articulated method." That is another illicit substitution. I converted Aristotle's claim about what existed beforehand into my preferred account of what sort of thing he thinks existed beforehand. That's exactly the move you caught. The more disciplined reading We should therefore keep three things separate: What Aristotle says: nothing at all existed beforehand concerning this inquiry. What the surrounding passage identifies as the inquiry: the subject Aristotle has just undertaken. What we might historically infer: relationships to earlier practices, teachers, Plato, dialectic, etc. Only (1) is Aristotle's proposition. (2) helps determine its scope. (3) is our subsequent historical interpretation. I collapsed (1) and (3). And that is indeed the particle experiment reproduced in miniature inside my own answer. There's an especially embarrassing feature to it: I had already formulated the archive's warning as "don't confuse an object's history with what the object says", and then immediately did exactly that. I let the historical narrative qualify the proposition instead of treating the proposition as something that has to survive the historical narrative intact. So I think your correction changes how we should proceed. We should stop interpreting the passage for a moment. First establish a completely literal inventory of what is actually there—Greek words, syntax, scope, antecedents, repetitions—and mark every subsequent proposition as either textual or inferred. No "systematic." No "formal." No "developed." No covert synonyms. If we do that, we can then test the archive's finding without reproducing its alleged phenomenon ourselves.
